title: Chris's rock bands: New Heavenly Blue, Sky King and the shelved Columbia record
summary: Chris tells of his rock bands, producers and guests on the Columbia record that was killed, after which his father invited him to play bass.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I’m glad you mentioned Darius because there’s this wonderful picture in the recent book about your father, A Life in Time and you three are standing behind your parents and it struck me, it looks, it’s the time of the era. It looks like Dave and Iola go to Haight Asbury. Because you all had really long hair and it just is so terrific to see that combination of the generations. And I’m not even sure what I’m trying to say except it’s a great pic.

Well it is funny, like because at that point Gerry Mulligan had really long hair and a beard and would wear bell bottoms and stuff and I think Maynard Ferguson. I mean I think there was a lot of establishment jazz guys, instead of fighting it just started going with the flow. Hey, and to your previous question, we were talking about Dan’s groups, I just wanted to say that when I was coming out of Interlochen I met all these young very good classical musicians that also loved rock & roll. And we had school bands and we said hey when we graduate we’re going to make a demo tape and see if we can get a deal.

And I very consciously knew that Dave was this really popular figure in jazz and I couldn’t compete in that world but I really wanted to have a really really creative rock & roll band. And the first thing we did was the group was called The New Heavenly Blue. We did a record on RCA. And then we did a record on Atlantic. And that evolved into a group called Sky King that we did a record on Columbia. And Madcat, the great harmonica player who I still play with and who played with two generations of Brubeck, he was in that band. And the Sky King thing was really quite cool but the legendary guitarist Steve Cropper produced us and we brought in the Tower of Power horns. At one point we were cutting our second record and the producer was Randy Brecker because they had just did the Brecker Brothers record with Skunk Funk and I could convince Bruce Lundvall — that’s one of the best produced records ever. If we have to have a producer let’s bring this guy in and then Bob James got involved and then Randy said, “Hey I want to bring in my friend” you know, “he’s a great background guy, and we’ll bring in a singer.” So it was like Whitney Houston’s mother Cissy Houston and some other amazing —

Right. And Jerry Bergonzi and also the background singer coach was this guy named Luther, Luther Vandross. And that record never even came out because the guy that was head of Columbia A&R, Mickey Eichner, was a complete idiot. I hope he hears this someday — oh he’s probably gone. But he was totally threatened to have Bob James on Tappan Zee Records come into the Columbia label fold. So just by bad luck the first project he could kill to show Bob James who had more power, it was our record. So despite it being ready to go and us touring the country and on radio stations saying, “We’re playing tracks from our new record” it didn’t happen. And so like half the guys in that group just quit the music business they were so demoralized. There’s a long story about lawyers selling us out and getting rewarded and all this kind of stuff. And my dad said, “Oh Chris, don’t be blue about that stuff” you know, “why don’t you just start playing bass with me?” So I did.
Not a bad solution to that problem.
